Changes Ahead at Renshaw Stationers
Local Business Section — By Ian Furlong
Millbrook, May 2
Frances Duvall, who opened Renshaw Stationers and has directed it ever since, will step back from daily management at the end of this month. Two members of her staff, Grace Abbott and Emil Kovacs, will take on the business jointly from June 1.
The store began in 1981 as a counter at the back of a printing company and has operated from its present address on the town's main business street for more than forty years. It supplies notebooks, file folders, and desk equipment to local offices and to schools across the district.
Ms. Abbott began as a delivery driver and now keeps the accounts, while Mr. Kovacs has taken orders at the front counter for eighteen years. Staffing will remain as it is. "The name above the door will not change, and neither will the way we do business," Mr. Kovacs said.
The store will close on May 18 while new shelving is installed inside, and it will reopen at the same address on May 26. Orders may be placed by e-mail throughout the closure, with no charge added for delivery. Deliveries themselves begin again on the reopening day, and a customer who needs an order before then may pick it up from the company's storage unit on Kestrel Lane.
Ms. Duvall will keep an office upstairs two mornings a week until December. "I would rather leave the store to people who helped build it than to a stranger," she said. "Our nine employees are all staying, and the work goes on as before."

Annual Comparison
Small-Office Copiers: How This Year's Ratings Were Made
Four submitted units, one rating still unfinished.
By our equipment testing editor, Naomi Pilcher
Four criteria decide the standing. Running cost per page carries the greatest weight, followed by output quality, then speed, then reliability in daily use. Last year speed came first, but readers told us that running costs matter more, so the order was changed for this cycle. Each criterion is placed in one of three bands, excellent, good, or fair, and the standard program runs ten weeks.
The LP-620 reached our test office eleven days after the testing period had closed, leaving no time to measure its running cost before we went to press. Under our standing rule, a unit that completes only part of the program is published with a provisional standing and may be rated again if its maker returns it.
The full grid appears opposite.
Test samples are bought at ordinary retail prices by this magazine unless the grid states otherwise.

Readers Ask
The maker of the LP-620 sent it back to you. Has its place in the grid changed? — from an office administrator
It has. The unit ran the complete program in April, and its running cost was measured for the first time, falling in the middle band. With all four criteria scored, the provisional entry is withdrawn, and the LP-620 now stands third, ahead of the ZR-88.

Do not start with the standing row, which is led by the unit that is cheapest to run. Choose the model that took the top band for output quality and also for reliability in daily use, and that stayed in the test the full ten weeks.
